name: The emigrants' wagon camp at the west approach
aka: the wagons beyond the Des Plaines Street line

documented_range.note: THE SEASON, NOT THE CAMP. The American of 13 June 1835 has the summer's emigrants already arriving; the range runs the emigrating summer. No source dates a wagon camp at the west approach or says there was one, and a party stopping a night or two before going on west was gone before anybody could write it down. What the range says is that on 1 July 1835 a party stood here. T-1804.

change_note: A wagon party's camp at the west edge of town. T-1804.

placement.position_note: THE GROUND IS A CONJECTURE AND THE SPOT IS OURS. 1835_camp_grounds.json offers the prairie edge beyond the westernmost platted corridor as where a wagon party stops without entering the town, and grades the candidacy conjectural: it rests on the direction of the traffic and nothing else. The camp stands at the western edge of the modelled ground, off the end of Randolph's drawn line: every sampled point of its ground between 1.32 and 1.33 m above the water plane on the committed heightfield; 134.1 m clear of the drawn edge of the nearest roadway (des_plaines); 48.0 m clear of the nearest committed footprint; 178.2 m clear of the nearest fence run. The point recorded is the camp's south-west corner, the footprint's origin at rotation 0, so the camp opens north. Placed by tools/place_camp_grounds_1835.py; L351.
placement.symbolic_location: On the prairie west of the Des Plaines Street line, between local E -700 and E -666 and N -236 to -202: beyond the last drawn street of the West Division, just north of the line Randolph would carry west, where the road out to the Des Plaines crossing left the town.

footprint.note: The camp's ground, 34.0 x 34.0 m. INVENTED in its extent: room for the pitches the form asks at the archetype's spacing, inside the ground the placer measured clear. L351.

tents.note: 2 WEDGE TENTS for a party of four wagons: the wagon beds carried the bedding and the tents took who did not fit. Invented. L351.

tent_kind.note: NO SOURCE DESCRIBES THE TENTS. The wedge tent is the smaller and cheaper of the two forms the archetype carries, and the one a family going on by wagon would carry. L351.

wagons.note: A PARTY OF FOUR WAGONS, invented: families came overland to Chicago from Indiana and Ohio in 1835 as well as by lake, and a party travelled together. L351.

brush_shelters.note: A lean-to of poles and cut brush, the cheapest roof there is. Invented. L351.

fire_rings.note: Two cooking fires inside the ring of wagons. Drawn out: no flame, no smoke, nobody at them (L1). L351.

woodpiles.note: Cordwood for the fires. Invented. L351.

baggage_heaps.note: What came off the wagons for the night. Invented. L351.

arrangement.note: A ring about the fires, because one party camps round its own fires with its wagons drawn up close.

canvas_condition.note: Patched: wagon covers and tents that had come hundreds of miles overland.

function.note: THE GROUND IS A CONJECTURE AND SO IS THE USE. The overland road came in from the west and the wagons that carried immigrant families came with it; the ground beyond the westernmost platted corridor is where a wagon party stops without entering the town. No committed source names a camp here. The candidacy rests on the direction of the traffic and nothing else. Built at the reconstructed tier on the owner's ask (T-1214) and labelled so; L351.

occupants.value: Nobody this layer counts. The transient model (T-1352/T-1353) counts the lake arrivals the papers describe and deals all 28 of its camp households to the landing place; no overland party is a row of it. So this camp seats nobody and moves no count. No figure is drawn (L1).
occupants.note: Seats nobody: see the value. T-1804.

citations.citation: The Chicago American. Vol. I, No. 1 (June 8, 1835) through Vol. I, No. 12 (August 29, 1835). Chicago, Ill.: T. O. Davis. Thirteen issues, OCR-assisted research transcriptions from page scans.

research_note: T-1804, the second piece of T-1214: the camps of the two conjectural grounds the owner named. The Native and Métis camps are NOT built here — T-1177 refused a count for them and the question is the owner's. WHAT WOULD REPLACE THIS: a letter or diary of an overland party reaching Chicago in 1835 saying where it stopped.
